original_value: Water vapor is an important driving factor in the related weather processes in the troposphere, and its temporal-spatial distribution and change are crucial to the formation of cloud and rainfall. Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) water vapor tomography, which can reconstruct the water vapor distribution using GNSS observation data, plays an increasingly important role in GNSS meteorology. In this paper, a method to improve the distribution of observations in GNSS water vapor tomography is proposed to overcome the problem of the relatively concentrated distribution of observations, enable satellite signal rays to penetrate more tomographic voxels, and improve the issue of overabundance of zero elements in a tomographic matrix. Numerical results indicate that the accuracy of the water vapor tomography is improved by the proposed method when the slant water vapor calculated by GAMIT is used as a reference. Comparative results of precipitable water vapor (PWV) and water vapor density (WVD) profiles from radiosonde station data indicate that the proposed method is superior to the conventional method in terms of the mean absolute error (MAE), standard deviations (STD), and root-mean-square error (RMS). Further discussion shows that the ill-condition of tomographic equation and the richness of data in the tomographic model need to be discussed separately.

result.paraphrase: Water vapor is a key driver of weather processes in the troposphere, and how it is distributed and changes over time and space is essential to cloud and rainfall formation. GNSS water vapor tomography, which reconstructs water vapor distribution from GNSS observation data, is playing an increasingly important role in GNSS meteorology. This paper proposes a method for improving the distribution of observations in GNSS water vapor tomography to address the relatively concentrated observation layout, allow satellite signal rays to pass through more tomographic voxels, and reduce the excess of zero elements in the tomographic matrix. Numerical results show that the proposed method improves water vapor tomography accuracy when slant water vapor calculated by GAMIT is used as the reference. Comparative PWV and WVD profile results from radiosonde station data show that the proposed method outperforms the conventional method in mean absolute error (MAE), standard deviation (STD), and root-mean-square error (RMS). Further discussion indicates that the ill-conditioning of the tomographic equation and the richness of data in the tomographic model should be considered separately.
